Je n'hésite pas, évidemment, à les unir dans ce cas. Ainsi on cherchera dans le dictionnaire luto, cuiller et non pas to, parce-que la particule lu prenant l'accent tonique, peut-être considérée comme faisant partie du mot. [p. 25] Bigni, s. pl. de ḳigni, s'écrit en un seul mot; la pc. a l'accent tonique de pénult. — Visages. V. ḳigni, — 2° Rosée. (accent sur la dernière syll.; ... Bika, s. pl. de ḳika. — Lits, v. ḳika. La pc. est unie au rad. en raison de l'accent de pénultième. [Ndinga-Koumba-Binza 2008: xxi] It should be noted that in this dissertation the marking of tones and other suprasegmental features at the orthographic level does not occur. ... H High tone ... L Low tone [p. 30] (ii) In an unstressed nominal prefix syllable (cf. Ndinga-Koumba-Binza 2000). [p. 159] in a phrase- or sentence penultimate syllable the duration of the vowel is longer than in other positions. [p. 164] (38) Rule 5: Vowel lengthening ... A single vowel is perceived long when it is in a penultimate syllable position of a phrase or sentence-final word. This rule is in line with a general rule in Bantu languages assigning length to the penultimate syllable of a phrase (cf. Watkins 1937: 10; Nurse 1996: 279; Childs 2003: 205).

new_statements.translation: Note, however, that there are monosyllabic nouns which place the penultimate tonic accent on the particle [class prefix] that precedes them. In such cases I do not hesitate to write them together. Thus one will look in the dictionary for luto 'spoon' and not to, because the particle lu, taking the tonic accent, may be regarded as part of the word. [p. 25:] Bigni, n. pl. of kigni, written as one word; the particle bears the penultimate tonic accent. — Faces. See kigni. — 2° Dew (accent on the last syllable).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (render of p. 12 = printed p. 6 of) and read the page scan myself. The p. 6 passage is there verbatim: "Remarquons cependant, qu'il y a des substantifs monosyllabiques, qui mettent sur la particule qui les précède, l'accent tonique de pénultième. Je n'hésite pas, évidemment, à les unir dans ce cas. Ainsi on cherchera dans le dictionnaire luto, cuiller et non pas to, parce-que la particule lu prenant l'accent tonique, peut-être considérée comme faisant partie du mot." (also at line 250 of the, with scanned noise). The p. 25 portion reads in print "Bigni, s. pl. de kigni, s'écrit en un seul mot; la pc. a l'accent tonique de pénult. — Visages. V. kigni,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Marichelle treats Vili as having a word-level tonic accent on the penultimate syllable; when the stem is monosyllabic, the penult is the noun-class prefix, which therefore carries the accent and is written together with the stem (lu-to 'spoon', bi-gni 'faces', bi-ka 'beds'). The modern instrumental work (Ndinga-Koumba-Binza 2008) does not describe word stress at all: it treats Civili as a tone language (H/L) and finds only phrase-penultimate vowel lengthening ('in line with a general rule in Bantu languages assigning length to the penultimate syllable of a phrase', p. 164), while referring in passing to 'an unstressed nominal prefix syllable' (p. 30). The 1902 'accent tonique' is most plausibly the Bantu penultimate lengthening/prominence rather than a contrastive stress system.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Marichelle p. 25 notes a minimal pair bigni 'faces' (accent on penult, i.e. on the prefix) vs bigni 'dew' with 'accent sur la dernière syllabe' — a final-accented word, probably a tonal distinction. Ndinga-Koumba-Binza 2008 p. 146: long vowels (except onomatopoeias) occur only in the first syllable of disyllabic words or the penultimate of polysyllabic words; word-final /a/ is reduced/devoiced (p. 30).
new_statements.domain_note: Marichelle: word level (citation forms of nouns in a dictionary; 'mot' = prefix + stem). Ndinga-Koumba-Binza 2008: lengthening is stated for the penultimate syllable of a phrase- or sentence-final word (phrase level), with tones as the lexical suprasegmental; no word-stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Marichelle 1902 describes the Vili of Loango (Congo-Brazzaville coast), the core variety of vili1238; Ndinga-Koumba-Binza 2008 works on Civili of Gabon (Mayumba/Nyanga area; Glottolog codes Civili de Mayumba under vili1238). The 1888 Ussel grammar calls the same Loango variety 'fiote' (not the Kakongo Fiote of Visseq 1889, which is Kongo).

new_statements.quote: [p. 10] La langue vilie a l'accent tonique. Les radicaux monosyllabes, à part de rares exceptions, laissent cet accent à leur particule [...] Ex. ḳika, le lit. Ḳi est long, parce qu'il prend l'accent. [p. 11] Les mots de deux syllabes, ont l'accent sur la pénultième. [...] Les mots de trois syllabes, ont l'accent sur l'antépénultième, en général. Futika, plier, fu est long. Les mots de quatre syllabes ont, en général, l'accent sur la première syllabe, et parfois sur la troisième. [...] Quand un mot, un verbe spécialement, prend un suffixe, l'accent se reporte sur la première voyelle du radical. Sāla, sālila, sālilila. Est excepté le suffixe anga, qui prend l'accent ; sálilānga.
new_statements.translation: [p. 10] The Vili language has the tonic (stress) accent. Monosyllabic radicals, apart from rare exceptions, leave this accent to their particle [class prefix] ... e.g. ḳika 'the bed': ḳi is long because it takes the accent. [p. 11] Words of two syllables have the accent on the penultimate. ... Words of three syllables have the accent on the antepenultimate, in general: futika 'to fold', fu is long. Words of four syllables have, in general, the accent on the first syllable, and sometimes on the third. ... When a word, a verb especially, takes a suffix, the accent goes back onto the first vowel of the radical: sāla, sālila, sālilila. Excepted is the suffix -anga, which takes the accent: sálilānga.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (classification tonal, rule empty; Marichelle 1902 p. 6 'substantifs monosyllabiques, qui mettent sur la particule qui les précède, l'accent tonique de pénultième'): the 1907 grammar repeats that particle rule verbatim in substance (pp. 8, 10) and adds the full placement rule, which is radical-initial rather than a general penult (trisyllables antepenult, quadrisyllables initial), ties accent to vowel length, and gives the suffix behaviour (-anga). It says nothing about lexical tone, so it neither supports nor denies the 'tonal' kind, which rests on Ndinga-Koumba-Binza 2008. If the 1902 line were read as 'penultimate stress language' this source would cont…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls on the first syllable of the radical (stem): hence penultimate in disyllables, antepenultimate in trisyllables, initial (occasionally third) in quadrisyllables; a monosyllabic radical throws the accent onto its class particle (prefix), which is then written joined to it (ḳi-ka, lu-to); derivational/verbal suffixes leave the accent on the radical's first vowel (sāla, sālila, sālilila) except -anga, which attracts it (sálilānga); the accented vowel is described as long. The class particle is otherwise unaccented. Nothing is said about tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned (sálilānga is printed with two marks, acute on sá and macron on lān, without comment)
new_statements.exceptions: 'rares exceptions' among monosyllabic radicals that do not cede the accent to the particle; four-syllable words 'parfois' accented on the third syllable; suffix -anga takes the accent
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe the Vili (Civili, 'tchi vili', fiote) of Loango / Pointe-Noire and the Kouilou coast, Congo-Brazzaville (Loëmbe p. 9: 'Majoritairement présents dans la région du Kouilou, au sud du Congo-Brazzaville'); Marichelle's is the Loango mission variety, same as his 1902 dictionary on which the catalog record rests.

tone_statements.quote: All nominals in the language fall into four distinct tone classes, each of which can appear with two different tone contours. This article shows that these two contours are systematically used to distinguish between definite and indefinite interpretations ... [p. 9, n. 5] Les tons modulés sur la voyelle radicale, qui porte l'accent, montrent qu'elle peut être associée à deux tons différents même lorsqu'elle est brève. Ces tons fusionnent lorsqu'ils sont identiques, en vertu du principe de contour obligatoire (OCP), mais la voyelle reste doublement associée.
tone_statements.translation: [n. 5] The contour tones on the radical vowel, which bears the accent, show that it can be associated with two different tones even when it is short. These tones merge when identical, by the Obligatory Contour Principle (OCP), but the vowel remains doubly associated.
tone_statements.locator: p. 7 (English abstract) and p. 9 footnote 5; tone-type table p. 9, section 5 'Neutralisations' pp. 18-23, conclusion p. 24
tone_statements.summary: Two tones H and B (L) with floating L and contour (modulated) tones on the accented radical vowel; four lexical tone types for nouns (A-D = *LL, *HL-long, *LH, *HL-short/*HH), each surfacing in two profiles (isolation vs 'this is a N' etc.) used for definiteness ('semantico-pragmatic' rather than positional tone cases); class 9 prefix yi- (old augment) drops with profile 2; accent on the radical…

tone_statements.citation: Blanchon, Jean Alain and Nsuka-Nkutsi, François (1984). Détermination des classes tonales des nominaux en ci-vili, i-sangu et inzèbi. Pholia 1. pp. 37-45.
tone_statements.quote: S'il en est ainsi, les nominaux du Ci-Vili auraient pour tous les thèmes de plus d'une syllabe deux types seulement: Type I ... Type II ... Le préfixe étant toujours haut et les syllabes suivant l'initiale du thème toujours basses, le critère de classement pertinent est uniquement le ton haut ou bas de la syllabe radicale. De fait, si l'on s'en tient, comme semble le faire Ndamba, aux formes de citation, tous les nominaux se répartissent bien entre ces deux types.
tone_statements.translation: If so, Ci-Vili nominals would have, for all themes of more than one syllable, only two types: Type I ... Type II ... The prefix being always high and the syllables after the theme-initial one always low, the only relevant classification criterion is the high or low tone of the radical syllable. Indeed, if one keeps, as Ndamba seems to do, to citation forms, all nominals divide neatly between these two types.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Nominal tonology only: H vs L (haut/bas); noun prefix always H in citation, syllables after the stem-initial one L; frames split stems into four underlying classes BB, BH, HB, HH; nothing on stress.

In Civili when the N precedes an unvoiced C and when it does not bear a tone8, this N disappears automatically in actual phonetic realization. ... 8 Case of syllabic Nasal. tone.quote: S'il en est ainsi, les nominaux du Ci-Vili auraient pour tous les thèmes de plus d'une syllabe deux types seulement: Type I ... Type II ... Le préfixe étant toujours haut et les syllabes suivant l'initiale du thème toujours basses, le critère de classement pertinent est uniquement le ton haut ou bas de la syllabe radicale. De fait, si l'on s'en tient, comme semble le faire Ndamba, aux formes de citation, tous les nominaux se répartissent bien entre ces deux types.
tone.translation: If so, Ci-Vili nominals would have, for all themes of more than one syllable, only two types: Type I ... Type II ... The prefix being always high and the syllables after the theme-initial one always low, the only relevant classification criterion is the high or low tone of the radical syllable. Indeed, if one keeps, as Ndamba seems to do, to citation forms, all nominals divide neatly between these two types.
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.summary: Nominal tonology only: H vs L (haut/bas); noun prefix always H in citation, syllables after the stem-initial one L; frames split stems into four underlying classes BB, BH, HB, HH; nothing on stress.
